fields.Front: Define data, database and mini-world in the slide (Elmasri and Navathe) wording.
fields.Back:
1. Data: known facts that can be recorded and that have an implicit meaning ('98' alone is a number; 'Homer's mark in CS3319 is 98' is data).
2. Database: a collection of RELATED data.
3. Mini-world: the part of the real world about which data is stored - the part of the organisation we want to model (a medical office, a retail business, a library).

fields.Front: Video 1 opens with a grocery list, a letter, a spreadsheet of grades, a student list and an Access screenshot and asks which are databases. What is the instructor's answer, and why is it a trick question?
fields.Back: All of them. A database is 'just a group of related data': the grocery list is related items, the letter's information is all related, the spreadsheet's rows are all students in the course. A database does NOT have to live in Access, MySQL or any DBMS.

fields.Front: Name five DBMS products mentioned in Lesson 1, and say what the instructor's mini-world example is.
fields.Back: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, DB2 and Access. Mini-world example: within Western, a database just for the Computer Science department - she calls narrowing the world like this 'divide and conquer'.

fields.Front: Describe the loop the instructor wrote in first year to read and write a flat file.
fields.Back: Read: while not at the end of the line, read until you hit a comma, read until the next comma, ... to the end of the line; put the values into variables or a record; go to the next line and repeat until end of file. Write: value, comma, value, comma, ... newline. Every program that touched the file contained this parsing logic.

fields.Front: In the flat-file world, what did the instructor call a 'database'? And what lesson does the student list with the date-like last column teach?
fields.Back: A group of related flat files together (students, courses, departments) that keep the organisation's data. The mis-read column teaches that you must know the CONTEXT of data to know what it means.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: a customer flat file has lines C1,Marge,Simpson,519-555-1234. Point to a piece of data, a record and the flat file - and say whether the digit 5 is data.
fields.Back: A whole field value such as the phone number 519-555-1234 (or the first name Marge) is data; Marge's whole line is a record; the file itself is the flat file. A single digit is NOT data - data is the smallest unit that carries meaning in the mini-world.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §1.1): what three implicit properties turn 'a collection of related data' into a database, and what four activities does a DBMS carry out on one?
fields.Back:
THREE PROPERTIES:
1. It REPRESENTS SOME ASPECT OF THE REAL WORLD - the miniworld or universe of discourse (UoD) - and changes in the miniworld must be reflected in it.
2. It is a LOGICALLY COHERENT collection with inherent meaning; a random assortment of data is not a database.
3. It is DESIGNED, BUILT AND POPULATED FOR A SPECIFIC PURPOSE, with an intended group of users and preconceived applications.
FOUR DBMS ACTIVITIES: DEFINING (specifying data types, structures and constraints; the description is stored as meta-data in the catalog), CONSTRUCTING (storing the data on a DBMS-controlled medium), MANIPULATING (querying, updating to track the miniworld, generating reports) and SHARING (several users and programs at once).

fields.Text: A DBMS is the {{c1::software package}} that facilitates creating and maintaining a computerized database; a database is the {{c1::data}} itself; a database system is {{c1::the DBMS together with the data}} (sometimes plus the applications).

A flat file is 'really just a {{c1::TXT (ASCII)}} file' in which each line holds one {{c1::record}}; a record is one occurrence of the thing the file stores, which she also calls an {{c1::instance}} (like one object of a class - the word record survives in C).

In the flat-file row 251012345,Homer,Simpson,CS there are {{c1::four}} pieces of data; the single character 2 is {{c1::not}} a piece of data because it has no {{c1::inherent meaning}}; the whole line is a record and the file is a flat file.

Textbook (Elmasri §1.1): the DBMS stores the database definition as a {{c1::catalog}} (or dictionary), and that descriptive information is called {{c1::meta-data}}. A {{c1::query}} normally only retrieves data, whereas a transaction may both read and write.
